6d130a5d492f3880f8a21e83.title_original: Trust, but Validate the Instrument: Auditing AI-Generated RTL Verification Plans on Authored Security-Regression Proxies
6d130a5d492f3880f8a21e83.excerpt: arXiv:2609.19844v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI-generated RTL verification plans can satisfy a provider schema yet fail at the boundary to trusted execution. We present SecTB-RTL, an auditable framework covering 31 tasks and 124 authored hardware-security regressions. A deterministic non-AI baseline killed 36, 75, and 78 mutants at increasing resource limits. The first confirmatory run (C1-R2) failed before model execution because the provider rejected its response schema. After a schema-only repair made without viewing outcomes, a separately frozen follow-up run (C1-R3) completed 1,860 calls. The provider accepted 1,857 responses, but only nine passed the production semantic validator. The generation and execution rules did not match. We therefore preserve the run as an instrument-validation incident and report no prompt-effect estimate. This incident shows that provider or schema acceptance does not establish execution validity. Compilation and coverage are only diagnostics; the exact saved artifact must pass the full production path. A subsequent follow-up is excluded because it did not satisfy the preregistered evidence-completeness gate and is treated only as future work. We release the benchmark, failure-preserving contract, incident provenance, and governance controls needed to prevent infrastructure behavior from being misreported as model behavior.

3abf6572c279469a2cdd2ca9.title_original: RLVR$^{2}$: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking
3abf6572c279469a2cdd2ca9.excerpt: arXiv:2609.23457v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is expanding from tasks with well-defined correctness signals, such as mathematics and code, toward multifaceted quality requirements specified by multi-dimensional rubrics. Since policy optimization consumes one scalar per rollout, rubric-based pipelines must map multiple criterion scores into a scalar reward. This aggregation is often treated as score scaling, but it implicitly determines how quality dimensions trade off during training. The prevailing practice, normalizing each criterion and taking a linear combination, assumes that cardinal score differences are comparable across criteria and that gains on one criterion compensate for failures on another; both assumptions are unreliable when criteria are semantically heterogeneous. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking (RLVR$^2$), a verifiable ranking paradigm for rubric-based RLVR. For each criterion, RLVR$^2$ converts rubric scores into criterion-specific within-group ordinal outcomes, recovers a latent utility from the resulting comparison matrix, and merges these utilities into one training signal. By retaining only within-group ordering and discarding raw score magnitudes, RLVR$^2$ avoids calibrating heterogeneous rubric scales. eb8a480ebaa1431822dff848.title_original: ThinkNet: Evolutionary Deep Ensembles for Efficient Motor-Imagery EEG Classification
eb8a480ebaa1431822dff848.excerpt: arXiv:2609.33967v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Practical assistive and rehabilitative brain--computer interfaces require subject-independent motor-imagery EEG (MI-EEG) decoders that generalize to new users under limited target-user data and constrained compute. We evaluate four-class BCI Competition IV-2a (session T) decoding with nine Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) folds, three seeds, seven fixed decoder entries, and a broader search over ten representative decoder families; the held-out subject is never used for normalization, hyperparameter, architecture, or ensemble-policy selection. In the fixed benchmark, the validation-selected compact decoder achieved 44.35$\pm$15.41\% accuracy with 4.9K parameters, 19 KB FP32 weights, and 0.99 ms batch-1 Orin CUDA inference. Across the broader search, compact models ($\leq$25K parameters) achieved higher mean held-out accuracy than mid-size and large alternatives after selected retraining (40.10\% vs. 35.09\% and 34.78\%). ec46d7e7dd3d590a5c8834ac.title_original: Graph World Models for Constrained Epidemic Policy Planning
ec46d7e7dd3d590a5c8834ac.excerpt: arXiv:2609.35545v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Epidemic policy planning often requires coordination between geographical regions, taking into account mobility-driven spillovers and how to make use of limited resources. Existing methods either lack action-conditioned models of coupled dynamics or cannot guarantee per-period feasibility. We present EpiMind, a graph world model framework for constrained epidemic policy planning across regions. A graph-factored recurrent state-space model generates joint policy-conditioned rollouts from regional latent beliefs, while graph-temporal ADMM optimizes regional interventions, enforces shared-resource feasibility through projection, and evaluates temporal specifications under the learned model. EpiMind reduces admission RMSE by 29% relative to graph-free dynamics modeling, plans within 1-5% of the best feasible constant policy with guaranteed shared-budget feasibility, and outperforms all deployable baselines across three resource budgets in real-context evaluation. These results demonstrate that graph-structured policy imagination with explicit constrained coordination supports effective epidemic interventions from learned dynamics.

625374f0da3a9e922d15f43c.title_original: MS-GLA: Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention for Addressing Representational Bottlenecks via Multi-Temporal Resolution
625374f0da3a9e922d15f43c.excerpt: arXiv:2609.35664v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gated Linear Attention (GLA) Transformers advance linear recurrent models through data-dependent gating, but face a core limitation: the fixed-capacity memory matrices across all heads operate at a single temporal resolution, where each token is processed individually, forcing them to simultaneously encode local syntactic patterns and long-range semantic structure, creating a representational bottleneck that gating alone is insufficient to resolve. We introduce Multi-Scale Gated Linear Attention (MS-GLA), which addresses this by distributing attention heads across multiple temporal resolutions. Coarser resolutions pool longer token spans naturally specializing toward long-range dependencies, while finer head groups retain sensitivity to local syntactic structure. A learnable, input-dependent fusion layer dynamically recombines head group outputs at each timestep, expanding effective memory capacity without increasing per-head state size. This multi-resolution decomposition draws on principles from Multi-Scale State-Space Models (MS-SSM), adapting them to the gated linear attention setting. We evaluate MS-GLA on language modeling, recall-intensive tasks, and long-context generalization. Across all settings, MS-GLA consistently achieves higher accuracy and lower perplexity than GLA at matched parameter counts, with up to 18.9% improvement on recall-intensive tasks and 9.5% lower average perplexity on language modeling be

418f027f9f259645d96de04c.title_original: FACT: Fidelity-Aware Construction of Articulated Twins
418f027f9f259645d96de04c.excerpt: arXiv:2609.37067v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Visually plausible articulated assets may still fail during contact interactions or exhibit inaccurate motion. We present FACT (Fidelity-Aware Construction of Articulated Twins), an agentic framework that progressively constructs articulated twins to improve geometry, contact, and dynamic fidelity. The agent drives an evidence--diagnosis--revision loop on a shared editable representation, selecting measurements and model edits using quantitative feedback, while numerical tools execute and validate the updates. It reconstructs editable articulated geometry from images through feature planning, targeted measurements, and diagnostic refinement. On this reference, it repairs collision proxies through task-aware local repartitioning before fidelity-constrained compression. Finally, it constructs response models from passive-response videos, using simulation residuals to guide model revision and constrained physical parameter fitting. Experiments show that FACT improves geometric reconstruction over baselines, enables more reliable interaction with simpler collision proxies, and better reproduces held-out physical responses than direct parameter inference.

d3e374534d5359639bd807cb.title_original: OpenCollab: A Multi-Agent Coding Framework with Programmable Collaboration and Controllable Runtime
d3e374534d5359639bd807cb.excerpt: arXiv:2609.38345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent coding systems are designed to tackle complex software engineering tasks through collaboration. However, existing evaluations typically assume configured organizations are followed faithfully, whereas reality differs. This behavioral gap, combined with differences in underlying system components, prevents clear attribution of observed gains. To this end, we introduce OpenCollab, a multi-agent coding framework that provides a unified infrastructure for programmable collaboration and controllable runtime. Specifically, OpenCollab unifies organization design, enforces experimental control on a shared runtime, and tracks execution through fine-grained event streams. On this basis, we define Adherence to quantify whether the declared organization is actually realized. Our experiments reveal that agents collaborate very differently across configurations: changing any single dimension shifts Adherence, from 47.2% to as high as 97.2%. Furthermore, extensive agentic coding benchmarks show that OpenCollab (Duo) establishes new SOTA performance compared to the mainstream harnesses such as Mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and Claude Code, showing that a well-designed organization can outperform strong existing harnesses, while OpenCollab's single-agent configuration uses the fewest tokens across all evaluated suites. OpenCollab establishes a unified multi-agent infrastructure for easy programmable collaboration an

a65c88afe2bfb18fd5ac2d28.title_original: Making LLMs Say What They Think: Measuring and Improving CoT-Interpretability Alignment
a65c88afe2bfb18fd5ac2d28.excerpt: arXiv:2609.38972v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) traces often serve as a proxy for how Large Language Models (LLMs) arrive at their answers. However, growing evidence shows that models' CoT often fails to reflect their internal computations and can be changed without affecting their final answers. In this work, we measure and improve the alignment between the reasoning described in an LLM's CoT and what it computes internally. We propose CoT-Interpretability Alignment (CIA), a metric that measures the agreement between a model's CoT traces and its internal reasoning strategies as detected by interpretability tools. We evaluate CIA on three tasks (two-hop question answering, hint intervention, and integer multiplication) across three LLMs, finding that LLMs exhibit limited alignment across all tasks (44.8-75.9%). We then experiment with improving CIA via post-training, setting both the task accuracy and parametric faithfulness signals as a reward. Experiments show that we can substantially improve CoT parametric faithfulness while maintaining or improving the task accuracy. We provide rich analysis, such as their generalization patterns. Our work provides both a framework for auditing CoT parametric faithfulness and a pathway toward making models' explicit reasoning more trustworthy. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yihuaihong/CIA-minimal-repro.

9c2a26cae38da127e12b97c3.title_original: Scale and Selection: What Makes Automatic Harness Evolution Work for Visual-Interface Robot Agents
9c2a26cae38da127e12b97c3.excerpt: arXiv:2609.39304v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When an off-the-shelf coding agent is used directly as a robot policy, observing a browser-based 3D interface through screenshots and acting by posing a virtual target gripper through a few tools, the agent's harness, its prompts, tools, and control rules, largely determines success, and until now it has been written by hand. We show that this harness can be improved automatically by another coding agent, the optimizer agent, and report two findings about what makes it work. First, the number of rollouts the optimizer agent sees per round governs whether the evolved harness generalizes: with rounds fixed, held-out success rises as the training batch grows from 5 to 100 rollouts, while small batches overfit the training tasks. Second, the optimizer agent must not be given free rein. Accepting every revision it proposes degrades the harness within a few rounds; a simple Champion-Challenger rule that promotes a revision only if it beats the incumbent on the same fixed cases turns the same loop into one that raises held-out success on LIBERO tasks from 51% to 67% over 30 rounds. Combining the evolved harness with a pretrained policy, through one tool that hands it control, reaches 71.2% on the RoboCasa365 leaderboard benchmark, 13.1 points above the best published entry. Automatic harness evolution for visual-interface robot agents is thus feasible, but its gains hinge on the rollout scale behind each decision and on how t

4125687b76dae7c18cc5d536.title_original: Useful to Whom? The Easy-versus-Coverage Boundary Moves with the Learner
4125687b76dae7c18cc5d536.excerpt: arXiv:2610.00221v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Is the same data equally useful to every learner? The question is whether the value of a training sample belongs to the sample or arises in its interaction with the learner. We test it with a selection experiment. Under a per-class budget, two kinds of samples compete for the slots: easy samples, which a short training run learns first, and coverage samples, which spread over the class in feature space. Easy samples win at small budgets and coverage samples at large ones, and the budget at which the winner flips, the crossover m0, can be measured. We ask whether m0 is set by the data or by the learner. To separate the two, we freeze the selected subsets and change only the learner that trains on them. On low-resolution ImageNet-100, doubling the width of a ResNet-18 moves the crossover from 57 to 85 samples per class on the same subsets. Enlarging the input grid from 32 to 64 pixels at fixed image information moves it from 85 to 57, and a single stride change reproduces or removes this shift. The grid shift shrinks as width grows. Under the native ImageNet-1k protocol, a 4x range of width moves the boundary by at most a few samples per class. On a Vision Transformer, coverage wins at every measured budget, even with easy subsets that work on the convolutional learner. The budget at which one kind of sample stops being the more useful kind therefore belongs to the learner, and the preferred regime of a selection strateg

6bf476bbe7ef9fed174079c8.title_original: Exploring More, Reasoning Better: Stepwise Risk-Sensitive GRPO for Diffusion Language Models
6bf476bbe7ef9fed174079c8.excerpt: arXiv:2610.00661v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by denoising a sequence or successive blocks, allowing several tokens to be revealed in parallel. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) reuses terminal feedback across these decisions, even as their conditioning context changes. We propose stepwise risk-sensitive GRPO (StepRS-GRPO), which varies the risk coefficient of the group-advantage transformation across denoising states while retaining the underlying trainer. For binary rewards, we show that this transformation is exactly a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages. A capability-based calibration suggests a coefficient scale, while endpoint and interpolation ablations guide schedule selection. Across multiple dLLM backbones and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, StepRS-GRPO improves both pass@1 accuracy and pass@k coverage over centered GRPO, while increasing answer diversity. In our ablation studies, mass-matched controls support the contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and the gains persist after matching the root mean square (RMS) of the advantages to that of centered GRPO. Reasoning-trace diagnostics further show that the diversity gains from StepRS-GRPO extend beyond final-answer strings.

0891408688fe770a291cbff1.title_original: Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents
0891408688fe770a291cbff1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.01892v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal agents commonly generate free-form reasoning before each action. For small models, limited model capacity can result in lengthy reasoning that provides little useful guidance for action generation while incurring substantial inference cost. To address this challenge, we introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as selection instead of open-ended generation. SSR represents recurring high-level reasoning as pre-specified, reusable natural-language candidates. At each turn, the model selects from these reasoning candidates based on their likelihoods given the current context, without requiring an auxiliary task head. Using pre-specified reasoning traces enables parallel scoring, where teacher-forced prefilling computes token likelihoods concurrently within and across candidates using a shared context KV cache. We evaluate SSR on seven multimodal search benchmarks using 2B and 4B models. Across multiple reinforcement learning objectives and supervised fine-tuning, SSR delivers significant efficiency gains without sacrificing task performance. SSR achieves an average success rate competitive with leading search agents of the same scale, while reducing per-turn reasoning latency by over 90% and total per-question model inference latency by 28-54%. Project page: https://zfy0314.github.io/ssr-webpage/.

bd28622f75abf038d0db8d7c.title_original: Evolving Hybrid Quantum-Classical Architectures for Image Classification
bd28622f75abf038d0db8d7c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.03220v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hybrid quantum classical neural networks integrate parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) with established deep learning architectures, but their performance depends strongly on the choice of quantum circuit architecture, a choice that remains largely manual. Most existing approaches rely on hand-designed or fixed circuit ans\"atze, requiring circuit structure, gate composition, and qubit connectivity to be specified in advance with no guarantee that they suit the task. This limitation is especially acute in image classification, where quantum circuits must transform features extracted by classical networks while remaining compact enough for practical training, requirements that generic, task-agnostic ans\"atze are unlikely to satisfy simultaneously. We extend EXAQC, an evolutionary framework for automated quantum circuit discovery, to image classification. EXAQC evolves PQCs as intermediate processing modules while retaining classical feature-extraction and prediction layers. On MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, EXAQC achieves 98.42%, 90.62%, and 85.47% accuracy, respectively, while using comparable gate counts to other quantum architecture-search methods. Against classical networks, evolved hybrid models maintain comparable accuracy with substantially fewer trainable parameters, reaching 85.68% on CIFAR-10 with over 25$\times$ fewer parameters than a 10-layer CNN. Encoding choice also matters: rotation-based encodin

80e2806292dac6bf808cee7b.title_original: GOTT: Object-centric Dexterous Manipulation with a Reusable Cross-Embodiment Primitive
80e2806292dac6bf808cee7b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.03861v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation models and large-scale human data provide rich sources of manipulation intent, but translating this intent into multi-fingered robot behavior remains difficult. Dexterous hands still lack a reusable low-level primitive that reliably establishes contact across tasks and embodiments. We propose GOTT, a reach-acquire-move framework built around a single cross-embodiment contact-acquisition primitive. Given a robot-agnostic object trajectory and a reach specification, GOTT first brings the hand near a task-relevant contact region. The shared closed-loop primitive then establishes stable contact from this approximate initialization, and a pose-conditioned controller tracks the desired object motion. Reach specifications may come from future-aware planning, external models, or human demonstrations, while the primitive and tracking backend remain unchanged. Simulation and real-world experiments show that GOTT is able to establish robust contact across diverse objects, arm-hand platforms, and seen and unseen hand morphologies. It also consistently improves end-to-end task success over open-loop grasp execution.

a79373265a7e72983302cc8b.title_original: Solving VeriContest with a Lean-Backed Rust Verifier
a79373265a7e72983302cc8b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.03994v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: VeriContest is a benchmark of 1007 competitive-programming problems in Rust, each with a Verus specification, a judge-accepted solution, and a Verus proof. Its authors report that proof generation is the bottleneck for frontier models: given the specification and the code, the best model produces an accepted Verus proof for 13.95% of the problems on the first attempt. We report on solving the same proof-generation task with Rust-Prover, a verifier for Rust backed by Lean 4. The Verus specification and the Rust code are restated and translated into Lean, each specification becomes a theorem, and agents prove the theorems with Lean's kernel as the final check. All 1325 theorems of all 1007 problems were proved. 1259 of them were proved in one run of under 32 hours on Claude Opus 5.5, at a median of 3.2 minutes and $1.17 per proof, and 70% of them on the first iteration. The restated specifications were checked against the benchmark's test suites, and reviewed where no suite applies. None was wrong or weakened. The translated Lean programs were run on 21,413 of the benchmark's test cases and produced the same output as the Rust programs on every one. Across four Claude and four GPT models at five reasoning-effort settings, every current frontier model proves nearly all of a ten-theorem sample at every setting, and more effort raises the cost without raising the number of proofs. The cheapest Claude setting, Sonnet 5.5 at

280512f81a7a8c54aa885d00.title_original: AgroGround: Multi-Granularity Grounded Recognition in Agriculture
280512f81a7a8c54aa885d00.excerpt: arXiv:2610.04425v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agricultural visual models are typically evaluated for either recognition or localization, but reliable diagnosis requires identifying what is present and localizing the evidence. Agricultural visual question answering (VQA) datasets carry rich semantic labels but rarely link them to image regions, and adding such annotations by hand is costly at scale. We introduce AgroGround, a large-scale dataset for grounded agricultural recognition: identifying plant diseases and other agricultural targets and localizing their image regions. An automated pipeline converts the labels of eight agricultural VQA datasets into annotations for disease lesions and whole objects, producing 794,850 instruction examples. Healthy images provide negative supervision for disease queries, teaching the model to return empty predictions. We fine-tune a shared vision-language model on known-target grounding instructions combined with instructions requiring both recognition and localization. We evaluate predicted identities, regions, joint correctness, and healthy-image abstention on 1,480 human-verified images disjoint from all training data. Grounding-only fine-tuning reduces recognition accuracy from 51.8\% to 29.1\%, while adding recognition-and-localization instructions raises it to 72.6\%. With images and annotations held fixed, combining the two formats raises joint accuracy from 19.2\% to 43.3\% at comparable grounding. Healthy negatives ra

dd631d0efbf93ea2a7253515.title_original: Video2World: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive World Modeling from Embodied Videos
dd631d0efbf93ea2a7253515.excerpt: arXiv:2610.04432v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Building interactive simulators from real-world observations is a promising way to scale embodied data, but current pipelines still rely heavily on manual environment construction and calibration. We study whether frontier foundation models and coding agents can automate this process end to end. We formulate \emph{autonomous video-to-simulation} as a software engineering task in which an agent observes an embodied video, constructs the corresponding simulated environment and robot behavior, and iteratively refines the result through execution feedback. To evaluate this capability, we introduce \textbf{Video2World}, a benchmark comprising 222 reconstruction instances derived from 189 robot and human demonstration videos. Video2World measures reconstructed worlds along geometric fidelity, dynamic fidelity, and functional correctness, capturing spatial perception, physical reasoning, and executable interaction. Evaluating 9 frontier coding-agent systems reveals a sharp improvement in Task success beginning with Claude Opus 5, rising from below 5\% to over 15\%, while substantial gaps to human-assisted reconstruction remain. We further find that worlds that look better could work worse: better visual fidelity does not always lead to higher task success. This echoes the broader gap between perceptual realism and factual correctness observed in generative models.

d89a99af7c6abf50cbf6f588.title_original: Green-Routed Neural Operators: Physics Determines Where the Network Reads
d89a99af7c6abf50cbf6f588.excerpt: arXiv:2610.05337v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We identify a mismatch between the physical role of transport fields in many PDEs and their usual role in neural operators: PDEs use them to select read coordinates, whereas neural operators typically treat them only as input values. We address this mismatch with the Green-Routed Neural Operator (GRNO), which uses the governing equation to determine where latent features are sampled. A parameter-free equation adapter evaluates the diagnostic relation and constructs a departure map whose values are the read coordinates. A multiscale encoder-decoder combines centered and routed reads of latent features to learn the complete finite-time update. Across five two- and three-dimensional PDE systems, GRNO achieves the lowest mean final relative $L^2$ error on four under 40-step autoregressive evaluation and remains competitive on Keller-Segel. Fixed-weight route interventions reveal strong dependence on direction and spatial alignment in four systems, with weak dependence in Keller-Segel. In independently trained ablations, GRNO achieves lower mean errors than variants that supply the transport field only as an input feature, substitute a learned displacement for the equation-specified route, or apply the route with a spatial misalignment, across all five systems. It also substantially outperforms directly advecting the physical state and learning the remaining update, indicating that equation-specified read coordinates provid

73609768f76e447726f02357.title_original: An Exploration of Attacks on AI Agent Systems
73609768f76e447726f02357.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As autonomous AI agents become more integrated into sensitive domains, it is crucial that single and multi-agent AI systems are secured. This paper investigates how prompt injection attacks can exploit both direct user inputs and inter?agent communication to leak sensitive information and trigger cross-agent infections. While our tests mostly highlight key vulnerabilities in single-agent systems, we also extend these attacks to multi-agent frameworks, investigating how weaknesses can propagate across agents. Our findings emphasize the need for more robust defenses as AI agents become more commonly embedded in real-world workflows.

7524a8847b8cd61d014bb837.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy-preserving order matching enables traders to discover and execute compatible orders while limiting disclosure of sensitive trading information. Existing systems span financial markets and blockchain-based asset exchanges and employ diverse market structures, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions, making their privacy guarantees difficult to compare. We present a systematization of privacy-preserving order matching covering 22 protocol families. We organize the order lifecycle into four phases: order representation and submission, order discovery and collection, order-matching, and settlement, and characterize each phase by protected and exposed information, access roles, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions. Our analysis shows that privacy is not a single protocol-level property: protecting selected order attributes or individual phases does not necessarily prevent leakage elsewhere in the lifecycle. We identify recurring trade-offs among privacy, functionality, trust, and verifiability, highlighting the challenge of achieving end-to-end privacy across the complete order lifecycle.

f56d42c9615bdbb15d747ae1.title_original: Organizational Context for the Enterprise Security Brain
f56d42c9615bdbb15d747ae1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents that investigate and decide on enterprise security reason over a machine-readable view of the environment: its assets, identities, configurations, relations, and findings. The correct judgment about an asset also depends on what the organization knows about it: who owns it, what business function it serves, which policy governs it, and which risks were accepted. Part of this knowledge can be inferred from machine state, such as an ownership tag; most of it is recorded by people in policies, audit reports, architecture diagrams, tickets, and conversations, outside machine state. We call this distance the organizational context gap. Closing it poses four challenges: extracting the right claims from heterogeneous organizational data and, at inference time, detecting claims made stale by live state, checking live state against the governing policy, and binding architecture diagrams, which carry the business logic, to live resources. We introduce organizational context as a layer of the enterprise security brain and define it with a taxonomy and six properties its representation must preserve. We then define a context model in which a claim carries one meaning, an attestation records each source that asserts it, strength is derived from live evidence at read time, and claims resolve onto the entities of the asset graph. On a production environment spanning AWS, Okta, Google Workspace, and GitHub, extraction recovers 0.80 of a

788845db7f66e193944a941b.title_original: HOMARD: Hammering Off-chip Memory via Aggregate power Rail Disclosure
788845db7f66e193944a941b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software-based microarchitectural attacks have mainly exploited timing differences to infer information from DRAM. However, defenses and optimizations can prevent timing-based approaches from resolving precise microarchitectural behaviors. We show that unprivileged millisecond- and milliampere-resolution power sensors on modern Arm SoCs can recover DRAM mapping functions and reveal the data dependence of memory accesses without timers. We present HOMARD, a methodology that reads DRAM activity from this telemetry, and two attack primitives. HOMARD-RE is a hierarchy-aware linear-algebraic method that reverse-engineers DRAM addressing functions from power alone. HOMARD-DATA recovers the Hamming weight of a fetched cache line through joint-power rail templating and secret byte values through correlation power analysis on the same rails. Across an AMD ZCU102, a Raspberry Pi 5, and a multi-chip-based LPDDR4 NVIDIA Jetson TX2, HOMARD-RE succeeds where row-buffer timing methods fail. On the Pi 5, HOMARD-DATA classifies 9 Hamming-weight levels at 81.5% accuracy and recovers secret bytes in minutes by correlating rail current with data-dependent bit toggling between neighbors in a row. Both primitives work with an architectural load or a mispredicted Spectre-RSB path on which no value is architecturally read. These results establish unprivileged power telemetry as an independent side channel for profiled microarchitectural attacks, partic

df8aa2cba200313827077136.title_original: Enabling Extended SGX Enclaves inside Confidential Virtual Machines
df8aa2cba200313827077136.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs), such as AMD SEV-SNP, and process enclaves, such as Intel SGX, provide workload protection against cloud threats. However, they strongly differ in TCB, deployment cost and speed, peer workload protection, resource sharing, fine-grained isolation and attestation, and programming capabilities. Nesting process enclaves within CVMs offers an optimal solution and an opportunity to address long-standing SGX limitations: lack of intra-enclave protection, expensive transitions and exception paths, slow enclave cloning, and a restricted programming model that limits Library Operating Systems (LibOS). This paper introduces TEEVisor, a CVM-resident architecture consisting of a security monitor and a kernel driver that leverages AMD SEV-SNP Virtual Machine Privilege Levels (VMPLs) to build hardware-protected, process-level enclaves inside a guest CVM with two modes: (1) an SGX binary compatibility mode to run unmodified SGX applications; and (2) a novel extended SGX~(eSGX) mode optimizing slow execution paths and offering richer enclave programming capabilities. On commercial AMD EPYC hardware, against native CVM execution, TEEVisor incurs under 5% overhead on compute- and memory-bound workloads, around 12% on I/O-heavy applications, and accelerates enclave cloning to a rate of 93~$\mu$s/MB of enclave size, demonstrating that eSGX semantics inside a CVM are practical for production use.

c0f88bef808e7123d5230d96.title_original: PVBRF-ID: Private, Verifiable and Byzantine-Robust Federated Intrusion Detection for Oilfield Enterprise Networks
c0f88bef808e7123d5230d96.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning allows dispersed oilfield sites to train a shared intrusion detector without pooling network traffic, yet its aggregation step forces a choice between privacy and robustness. Byzantine-robust rules must read each update in the clear, whereas secure aggregation hides updates from the checks that detect poisoning. We present PVBRF-ID, a two-server protocol in which sites secret-share their updates and the servers jointly test each update's norm and its cosine similarity to a reference computed on a small clean root set, revealing one accept bit per site. Commitments, Merkle roots and a homomorphic audit make the inclusion of accepted updates publicly verifiable. On a 15-class Edge-IIoTset task with ten sites holding differently distributed data and ten random seeds, PVBRF-ID matched FedAvg on clean data (macro-F1 0.708 vs. 0.706) and withstood sign-flip attacks (0.696 vs. 0.091). Against an adaptive attacker controlling 30% of sites, PVBRF-ID with secure clipping reached 0.641, whereas FedAvg fell to 0.046; plaintext multi-Krum remained higher by 0.052. An update-inference attacker recovered each site's class mix from plaintext updates (Spearman correlation 0.81) but not from one server's view. Backdoors passed the filter, and noise-based mitigation gave only heuristic protection. The implementation uses Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3, 30 rounds and 10 seeds.

e208cccd2e97368596656057.title_original: Better Batches, Better Privacy: Random Allocation for DP-BandMF
e208cccd2e97368596656057.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The current state of the art for batch selection and noise addition in differentially private training is a combination of DP-BandMF (informally, DP-SGD where the noise added in two different steps can be correlated if the steps are within $b$ of each other) and privacy amplification by sampling via Monte Carlo accounting. First, whereas prior batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF were inspired by Poisson sampling, random allocation is known to outperform Poisson sampling for DP-SGD. We therefore propose and analyze new batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF inspired by random allocation, improving RMSE by up to $1.85\times$ over previous work. Second, Monte Carlo accounting typically requires drawing $\Omega(1/\delta)$ samples from a privacy loss distribution, making accounting costly. We increase sampling and scoring throughput by two orders of magnitude through a carefully optimized GPU implementation. Finally, previous work chose the DP-BandMF strategy matrix and the batch selection strategy independently. We give a simple framework for choosing these parameters jointly, reducing RMSE by up to $13.4\%$ over fixed strategy matrices.

9d766db4f0d8db59a14bb0b8.title_original: Onions in the ATmosphere: Decentralizing Trust in Identity
9d766db4f0d8db59a14bb0b8.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiple approaches have been implemented for identities that associate meaningful identifiers, such as domain names, with self-authenticating identifiers, such as onion addresses. While these approaches offer various advantages both from identifier meaningfulness and from identifier self-authentication, identifier association itself is subject to blocking, hijack, fingerprinting, and other forms of surveillance and manipulation. So too are the resources associated with an identity comprising a meaningful identifier and a self-authenticating identifier. This paper describes ongoing work on two such approaches to self-authenticating meaningful identity (SAMI): associating a registered domain name with an onion address (onion association) and associating an atproto handle with a decentralized identifier (DID association). We present both the application of already implemented and published means of secure onion association to DID association and the combination of both in a single identity. Finally, we describe grounding identity association and integrity in contextual trust, wherein trusting attestations of identity relies on contextual relevance of an attestor to the identity rather than relying only on structural authority, for example as embodied in the traditional centralized infrastructure.

56547585a5c0e440ef25f853.title_original: Power, Performance, and Area of HPC-Based Malware Detectors: An FPGA and Open-PDK ASIC Study
56547585a5c0e440ef25f853.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware malware detectors (HMDs) classify programs as benign or malicious based on hardware performance counter (HPC) data. Previous studies have shown that ensemble classifiers outperform other classifiers on detection metrics. However, the area, power, and timing costs of HMDs remain open questions. We address these questions across a comprehensive design space comprising multiple classifier families, variable HPC sets, and ensemble learning methods. We designed a pipeline to reconstruct selected trained models, generate synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) implementations, validate each design against a bit-accurate golden model, and evaluate the implementations. The results show that tree- and rule-based detectors achieve the highest detection performance with nearly an order of magnitude less area and several times lower energy than function-based classifiers. Reducing the number of HPC inputs to fit a processor's concurrent-counter limit preserves detection performance while substantially reducing area, power, and delay.

22a09b12df5e72da3ee60462.title_original: Vulnerable Models in the AI Supply Chain: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Propagation, and Usage Patterns
22a09b12df5e72da3ee60462.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has established a complex supply chain, but many of these shared artifacts harbor severe vulnerabilities such as insecure serialization and architectural backdoors. We bridge this gap by conducting a large-scale empirical study on the usage and propagation of 16,977 known vulnerable models on HuggingFace flagged by InsightDB. We track their prevalence across GitHub repositories, software packages, fine-tuning chains, and deployed applications. Our analysis reveals that, despite being publicly flagged, these vulnerable models appear in over 21,000 code locations across more than 5,000 open-source repositories, with 3,757 distinct flagged models (22.1\%) actively referenced in at least one project. To understand how these models are integrated in code and identify recurring usage patterns, we categorize and analyze the recurring patterns surrounding them via a customized pipeline that combines Code Property Graphs extraction with a tailored Frequent Subgraph Mining approach. Across all patterns, we find no evidence of provenance verification or model sanitization logic, with developers frequently bypassing security parameters or delegating trust

22a09b12df5e72da3ee60462.summary_ko: 연구진은 HuggingFace에 공개된 취약한 AI 모델들이 오픈소스 저장소와 애플리케이션에 어떻게 채택되고 전파되는지 대규모 실증 연구를 수행했다. 분석 결과 취약한 모델들이 수천 개의 저장소에서 사용되고 있으며, 개발자들이 보안 검증 없이 이를 통합하고 있어 애플리케이션 계층의 가드레일 강화가 시급한 것으로 나타났다.

d62c4bdbdaf416b79e6d1ee1.title_original: Sample-Preserving Search-to-Decision Reduction for Noisy Linear Equations over Large Moduli
d62c4bdbdaf416b79e6d1ee1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Noisy Linear Equations problem involves finding the solution to a random linear system over a finite field given noisy evaluations. This is a generalisation of various learning problems widely used in cryptography, including Learning with Errors (LWE), Learning with Rounding (LWR), and Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). We present a new sample-preserving search-to-decision reduction for Noisy Linear Equations that has complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log q, q/\sigma)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the secret, $m$ is the number of samples, $q$ is the modulus, and $\sigma$ is the magnitude of the noise (defined suitably for the kind of noise involved). In particular, this implies search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR that run in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ even if the modulus $q$ is exponentially large, as long as the noise-to-modulus ratio $\sigma/q$ is non-negligible. Our reduction works for prime moduli $q$. If $q$ is composite, it instead produces a list that contains a small multiple of the solution. Prior to this work, known search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR either did not preserve the parameters of the problem (i.e., $m$, $n$, $\sigma$, and $q$), or had complexity that scaled polynomially with either $\sigma$ or the largest prime factor of $q$.

423e809efc118265092ae53b.title_original: AgentValve: Sybil-Resilient Payment Authorization for Permissionless AI Markets
423e809efc118265092ae53b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents increasingly select and pay service providers without human review. In emerging permissionless markets, however, adversaries can create inexpensive identities and fabricate feedback to inflate provider reputation, making reputation-based payment authorization vulnerable to Sybil attacks and exposing clients to unbounded financial loss. This paper presents AgentValve, a protocol for Sybil-resilient payment authorization in permissionless AI markets. AgentValve builds on a trust network that represents reputation as finite capacity in a directed graph and authorizes payments through trust paths with sufficient available capacity. A smart contract atomically reserves the capacity supporting each admitted payment, bounding honest agents' payment exposure by the capacity they extend into the adversarial region, and thus creating identities or interactions entirely within that region cannot increase this bound. To limit capacity depletion by malicious senders, AgentValve combines payment-backed capacity creation with bounded route length, preventing attackers from depleting honest capacity without incurring corresponding payment costs. AgentValve further decouples off-chain route discovery from on-chain verification and introduces a witness-commit mechanism that reduces route verification to linear work while requiring only constant persistent state per admitted payment. We implement a AgentValve prototype and evaluate it us

2ab0c4eac5cb8ae20a86b508.title_original: WaveMark: Robust Wavelet-Domain Image Watermarking for Diffusion Models
2ab0c4eac5cb8ae20a86b508.excerpt: arXiv:2610.12952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Image watermarking enables provenance tracing for photorealistic images generated by diffusion models. However, state-of-the-art (SOTA) removal attacks can suppress embedded signals with little perceptual degradation. This vulnerability limits the effectiveness of watermarks for intellectual property protection and misuse attribution. We propose WaveMark, a novel wavelet-domain watermarking method that embeds messages in a diffusion model's initial noise. To support robust recovery from perturbed carriers, WaveMark distributes keyed replicas of message bits across spatial positions, wavelet orientations, and scales. Each carrier groups coefficients from four latent channels and encodes a randomized bit through magnitude projection, providing an explicit decoding margin. We evaluate WaveMark with SD2.1 on SDP and MS-COCO Captions under 14 attacks. WaveMark achieves 100.0% bit accuracy (BA) without attacks, while maintaining image quality comparable to the evaluated baselines. Under SOTA MarkNull and MarkNull-A, it retains over 88% BA, outperforming all baselines.

9cf022621fc2592d8ab34a5b.title_original: Post-Quantum Session Establishment for Matter over Thread: Message Size, Transport, and Protocol Options
9cf022621fc2592d8ab34a5b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matter's first post-quantum change protects device attestation with ML-DSA, but its operational handshake, CASE, still derives session keys from P-256 ECDH, so recorded traffic can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. A byte-exact model of the CASE messages shows that a drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB and that no fully post-quantum configuration built from FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms fits the message limit. A Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter source constants, shows that sending these messages as fragmented IPv6 datagrams causes spurious retransmissions whenever a message and its reply outlast Matter's retransmission timer. At three to four hops the drop-in handshake then takes 1.8 to 2.6 times longer than with a selective-repeat block transfer, with or without interference, and up to 33% of handshakes with sleepy devices fail; raising the timers does not remove the effect. Caching certificate chains and authenticating the device with a pre-distributed ML-KEM key reduce the handshake to 6.1 kB and 44 ms of device computation. 1c43a333ac61d2e3090c4330.title_original: Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
1c43a333ac61d2e3090c4330.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, for any fixed $\kappa>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, the same time bound holds with errors bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ and only $O(n/\ln\ln q)$ samples. Earlier, it was known that Kirchner and Fouque's algorithm could solve LWE with these parameters in subexponential time with a much larger number of samples $m = \Omega(n\log{n})$ [HKM18]. Ducas et al. [DEL25] showed that an adaptation of this algorithm could solve the corresponding dual, the $\mathrm{SIS}^{\infty}$ problem, with a suitable norm bound $q/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ and $m=n+\omega(n/\ln\ln n)$ variables in subexponential time. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.

a4c6055fd6645bd3aa6707ec.title_original: Space Over Statistic, Retraining Over Ranking: Auditing Training Labels Under Label-Only Backdoors
a4c6055fd6645bd3aa6707ec.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Some backdoor attacks never touch an image. FLIP only changes labels: on CIFAR-10, flipping 3% of them makes a ResNet-32 send 99.7% of triggered source-class images to the attacker's class. We answer with a controlled swap: we keep the test, the labels and the metric fixed, change only the feature space, and judge each defense by retraining the victim on what it keeps. The space decides. On dog$\to$cat the same nearest-neighbor check scores AUROC 0.546 on the poisoned model's features, 0.967 on frozen DINOv2 features that never saw a label, and 0.995 on the same network trained on clean labels, an oracle control rather than a defense. 9ca6406df6c9ec22d1abaa95.title_original: CAPE - Context-Aware Prioritization Engine for Vulnerability Scoring and Management
9ca6406df6c9ec22d1abaa95.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability patching is critical for safeguarding an enterprise's software ecosystem from cyber attacks. However, patching requires adequate preparation for potential system downtime and for unforeseen effects of the patched software on a live system. Thus, effective risk mitigation requires prioritization strategies that explicitly account for the operational context of the affected software. While vulnerability prioritization based on Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, can help, their differing goals and methodologies often lead to inconsistent, context-unaware decisions resulting in mis-allocated remediation efforts. In this work, we present the Context-Aware Prioritization Engine (CAPE), a vulnerability analysis framework that enriches each vulnerability scanner report of vulnerabilities (CVEs) with deployment-specific evidence. This evidence is used to perform vulnerability reachability, centrality, and exploitability analysis, producing a ranked priority score for the effective distribution of remediation effort. We evaluate CAPE on 30 open-source agentic applications comprising 6,138 scanner-reported CVEs. Our evaluation shows that a significant majority of CVEs are not reachable and exploitable which results in significant disparities between CAPE and context-free baselines - the CVSS, EPSS, and KEV. 954d078746726fcfc765bc2b.title_original: The Limits of Query Monitoring against Distributed Model Extraction
954d078746726fcfc765bc2b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model providers now face distillation campaigns run through thousands of accounts, each of which looks like an ordinary user. We make this precise, show that a small but positive difference between campaign and users buys a detection time rather than detectability, and identify the campaign that is hardest to detect. e10437f835bfb0f483301cc8.title_original: Safety Graph: When Safety Responses Become Attack Surfaces in Cyber-Physical Systems
e10437f835bfb0f483301cc8.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern industrial control systems (ICS) are susceptible to cyber attacks triggering safety failures in the operational technology (OT) layer. The traditional way to mitigate any failure in OT is to implement safety responses. However, we show in this work that these responses can open up new attack surfaces, thereby vastly expanding the scope of lateral movement. Existing frameworks model cyber-to-physical escalation but provide no mechanism to reason about how these safety responses to OT-failures can trigger new cascading cyber attacks in the Information Technology (IT) layer. We provide a sound and complete compilation of SG to a classical AI planning problem, performing plan search using A* to find cross-layer cascade paths. Through a Web3D modeling and simulation of the Tennessee Eastman chemical process plant, which is a widely used chemical engineering benchmark serving as a standard for testing control, monitoring and fault propagation, we demonstrate that the planning compilation of SG automatically discovers safety-response-induced lateral movements, and identifies the responsible barriers that are unidentifiable under existing models. d3620fa3282ee60cc1bf7fa7.title_original: Understanding Verification Vulnerabilities in Cross-chain Bridges: An Empirical Study
d3620fa3282ee60cc1bf7fa7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid development of blockchain technology, numerous heterogeneous blockchains have emerged, each featuring distinct architectures, consensus mechanisms, and application ecosystems. Cross-chain bridges have consequently become a critical infrastructure component, typically relying on smart contracts to facilitate message passing and asset transfers across heterogeneous blockchains. Unlike single-chain contracts, bridge contracts introduce additional verification logic to validate external-chain data, such as state proofs, message sender identities, and signatures. However, correctly implementing such logic is challenging. We refer to vulnerabilities that violate the security guarantees of cross-chain verification as Cross-chain Verification Vulnerabilities (CVVs). To characterize CVVs, we conduct the first systematic empirical study of this vulnerability class. By analyzing 588 security audit reports from 36 real-world cross-chain bridge projects, we derive 11 CVV patterns and organize them into 5 high-level categories according to the affected verification properties. Following this taxonomy, we construct a CVV dataset containing 830 vulnerability instances across 786 contract files. The dataset establishes mappings among audit reports, audited source-code versions, affected source files, and CVV-pattern labels. We then assess existing detection approaches. 3a91b9805f8686543af7d35c.title_original: Understanding and Mitigating Cross-Session Attacks via Persistent Artifacts in Agent Skill Composition
3a91b9805f8686543af7d35c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills extend the capabilities of AI agents by bundling instructions, code, and resources into reusable packages. During skill execution, agents may produce or modify artifacts, such as files, configurations, and cached data, that are reused by other skills in later sessions. Since these artifacts can persist across sessions and later be accessed by other skills, they introduce a new attack surface that can be exploited to influence subsequent executions. In this work, we investigate cross-session composition attacks in skill-based AI agents and develop a runtime defense against them. Specifically, we characterize three attack mechanisms, namely Instruction Propagation (IP), Data Boundary Violation (DBV), and Evidence Poisoning (EP), through which malicious effects propagate across skill executions via persistent artifacts. To evaluate whether existing agents can resist these attacks while completing legitimate tasks, we construct SkillRelayBench, a benchmark of 270 adversarial cases drawn from 30 cross-session skill-composition scenarios across ten domains. Our evaluation of seven models across Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code reveals attack success rates (ASR) ranging from 46.7% to 77.4% and attack chain success rates (ACSR) ranging from 35.6% to 61.1%. ae589bf80ccda56cc3d4eb73.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inside a federated learning system a participant can quietly study the shared model and learn about others' private data. Against a purely passive attacker the only signal is timing, and it is not robust: a cohort-relative test detects only in low-jitter conditions while a false-positive-free per-client baseline is blind, so no configuration delivers both. 85b4f077bde14e7ee301a42a.title_original: Secrets in Preamble: Practical and Robust PHY Information Hiding for Wi-Fi
85b4f077bde14e7ee301a42a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical layer (PHY) information hiding refers to the concealment of secrets within PHY waveforms without compromising the integrity of the primary communication link, thereby enabling critical applications such as covert communication, PHY steganography, and watermarking. The widespread deployment of Wi-Fi has motivated substantial research interest in hiding secrets within Wi-Fi waveforms. However, existing Wi-Fi information hiding approaches suffer from two limitations: restricted steganographic capacity and insufficient robustness against environmental variations, both of which severely constrain practical deployment. This work proposes to embed secrets within the Wi-Fi legacy short training field (L-STF). The designed method preserves the autocorrelation properties of Wi-Fi L-STF, ensuring that packet detection and coarse frequency offset compensation functionalities remain uncompromised. The secret embedding and extraction processes employ a pair of neural networks designed to learn optimal embedding rules and maximize steganographic capacity. We developed a prototype system and conducted comprehensive experiments across both indoor and outdoor environments. Experimental results show that our method can reliably embed 46 secret bits within Wi-Fi packets across diverse channel conditions, achieving significantly enhanced steganographic capacity and environmental robustness. f61b4a46d7bb5fdf1f686171.title_original: Towards Safe World Models: Risks, Defenses, and Evaluation
f61b4a46d7bb5fdf1f686171.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models support planning, control, learning from imagined experience, and model-mediated evaluation by predicting action-conditioned consequences. Their safety cannot be inferred from predictive accuracy alone: errors in observations, state and memory, dynamics, evaluation, execution, or feedback can propagate into unsafe decisions and persist through updates. This work organizes the literature on world-model safety around a six-stage lifecycle covering data and observations, state and memory, dynamics and imagination, evaluation and planning, action and control, and feedback and update. We synthesize non-adversarial failures, attacks, defenses, evaluation protocols, benchmarks, and deployment conditions, and distinguish evidence directness from outcome level. The current evidence corpus contains 163 cited works. We use the framework to identify where claims are supported, where attribution remains unresolved, and which measurements are needed to connect model-level behavior to closed-loop and operational safety.

4a0116980aaf91869af577e1.title_original: EviRepair: Evidence-Driven Agents for Reliable Vulnerability Repair
4a0116980aaf91869af577e1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agent-based approaches for repository-level automated vulnerability repair (AVR), showing promising repair capabilities. However, an important issue has received limited attention: how can we ensure that the evidence generated during the repair process is reliable enough to support accurate vulnerability understanding and patch generation? In this paper, we propose EviRepair, an evidence-driven multi-agent framework for repository-level AVR. EviRepair introduces evidence review into the repair process by enabling agents to collaboratively collect vulnerability evidence, verify evidence consistency, and construct a reviewed vulnerability model for patch synthesis and validation. Extensive experiments on PatchEval and SecBench benchmarks with multiple agent frameworks and LLMs demonstrate that EviRepair consistently outperforms existing agent-based baselines, achieving average improvements of 16.37% and 40.33% in resolved rates on PatchEval and SecBench, respectively. Codes are available at https://github.com/lly-s/EviRepair

7f638743275234bec4d44f66.title_original: APEX-Harm: Evaluating Agent Safety in Shared Professional Workspaces
7f638743275234bec4d44f66.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Professional agents increasingly work through command-line interfaces and multiple tools over shared workspaces containing files, messages, and business applications. These environments create safety risks that are difficult to capture with attacks placed at a single, known read location. Each task contains 115 to 328 files, together with email, calendar, chat, document, spreadsheet, PDF, and code-execution tools exposed through MCP servers. We evaluate 12 frontier models on 180 task instances per model. Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 have the lowest overall attack success rates (8% and 20%), while task-specific script replacement and attacker-provided generic script attacks remain substantially more effective, averaging 81-84% and 73% attack success, respectively. Gemini 3.8 Flash achieves the highest mean task score (0.877) while still exhibiting a 33% attack success rate.
